¶

'''belikely†''' (bẹ̄-līk′li), ''adv.'' [See ''belike.''] Probably.

{{smaller block|Having ''belikely'' heard some better words of me than I could deserve. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Account of Himself.}}}}

'''belime''' (bẹ̄-līm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lime''<sup>1</sup>.] To besmear or entangle with or as with bird-lime. ''Bp. Hall.''

'''belinkedness''' (bẹ̄-lingkt′nes), ''n.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''link''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ness.''] In ''math.'', the number of times one branch of a link must be passed through the other in order to undo it.

'''belittle''' (bẹ̄-lit′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''belittled'', ppr. ''belittling.'' [First in U. S.; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''little.''] '''1.''' To make small or smaller; reduce in proportion or extent. [Rare.]—'''2.''' To cause to appear small; depreciate; lower in character or importance; speak lightly or disparagingly of.

'''belittlement''' (bẹ̄-lit′l-ment), ''n.'' [< ''belittle'' + ''-ment.''] The act of belittling, or detracting from the character or importance of a person or thing.

{{smaller block|A systematic ''belittlement'' of the essential, and exaggeration of the non-essential, in the story. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XX. 370.}}}}

'''belive<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. i.'' [ME. (rare), < AS. ''belīfan'' (pret. ''belāf'', pl. ''belifon'', pp. ''belifen'') (= OS. ''bilībhan'' = OFries. ''bilīva'', ''blīva'' = D. ''blijven'' = OHG. ''bilīban'', MHG. ''belīben'', ''blīben'', G. ''bleiben'' = Goth. ''bileiban''), remain, < ''be-'' + *''līfan'' (pret. ''lāf''), remain. Hence the causal ''beleave'', q. v., now also obsolete: see ''leave''<sup>1</sup>.] To remain.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|belie|513|belive}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|<poem>Thou dost ''belie'' him, Percy, thou dost ''belie'' him:
He never did encounter with Glendower.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 3.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Who is he that ''belies'' the blood and libels the fame of his own ancestors?
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Senate, May 7, 1834.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The clamor of liars ''belied'' in the hubbub of lies.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, iv. 9.}}</poem>}}
'''2.''' To give the lie to; show to be false; contradict.
{{smaller block|<poem>Their trembling hearts ''belie'' their boastful tongues.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}
Novels (witness ev’ry month’s review)
''Belie'' their name, and offer nothing new.
{{right|''Cowper'', Retirement.}}</poem>}}
'''3.''' To act unworthily of; fail to equal or come up to; disappoint: as, to ''belie'' one’s hopes or expectations.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shall Hector, born to war, his birthright yield,
''Belie'' his courage, and forsake the field?
{{right|''Dryden'', Hector and Androm., l. 109.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Tuscan Valerius by force o’ercame,
And not ''bely’d'' his mighty father’s name.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid.}}</poem>}}
'''4.''' To give a false representation of; conceal the true character of.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Queen.'' For heaven’s sake, speak comfortable words.
''York.'' Should I do so, I should ''belie'' my thoughts.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 2.}}</poem>}}
'''5†.''' To fill with lies.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis slander, . . . whose breath
Rides on the posting winds, and doth ''belie''
All corners of the world. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 4.</poem>}}
'''6†.''' To counterfeit; mimic; feign resemblance to.
{{smaller block|<poem>With dust, with horses’ hoofs, that beat the ground,</poem>}}
<poem>And martial brass, ''belie'' the thunder’s sound.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Astræa Redux.}}}}

'''belief''' (bē-lēf′), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''beleef'', ''beleeve'', < ME. ''beleve'', ''beleafe'', with prefix ''be-'' (as in ''believe'', q. v.), parallel with the earlier ''leve'', by apheresis for ''ileve'', < AS. ''geleáfa'' = OS. ''gilōbho'' = D. ''geloof'' = MLG. ''gelōve'', ''gelōf'' = OHG. ''giloubo'', MHG. ''geloube'', G. ''glaube'', masc., = Goth. ''galaubeins'', fem., belief, < ''galaubs'', dear, valuable: see ''believe''.]   '''1.''' Confidence reposed in any person or thing; faith; trust: as, a child’s ''belief'' in his parents.
{{smaller block|<poem>To make the worthy Leonatus mad,
By wounding his ''belief'' in her renown.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' A conviction of the truth of a given proposition or an alleged fact, resting upon grounds insufficient to constitute positive knowledge.
{{smaller block|Knowledge is a state of mind which necessarily implies a corresponding state of things; belief is a state of mind merely, and does not necessarily involve a corresponding state of things. But ''belief'' is sometimes used to include the absolute conviction or certainty which accompanies knowledge.}}
{{smaller block|Neither do I labor for a greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a ''belief'' from you, to do yourself good, and not to grace me. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Belief'' admits of all degrees, from the slightest suspicion to the fullest assurance. {{right|''Reid.''}}}}
{{smaller block|He [James Mill] uses the word ''belief'' as the most general term for every species of conviction or assurance; the assurance of what is before our eyes, as well as of that which we only remember or expect; of what we know by direct perception, as well as of what we accept on the evidence of testimony or of reasoning. {{right|''J. S. Mill.''}}}}

{{smaller block|By a singular freak of language we use the word ''belief'' to designate both the least persistent and the most persistent coherence among our states of consciousness,—to describe our state of mind with reference both to those propositions of the truth of which we are least certain, and to those of the truth of which we are most certain.
{{right|''J. Fiske'', Cosmic Philos., I. 61.}}}}

'''3.''' Persuasion of the truth of a proposition, but with the consciousness that the positive evidence for it is insufficient or wanting; especially, assurance of the truth of what rests chiefly or solely upon authority. {{smaller|(''a'') In this sense, the word sometimes implies that the proposition is admitted as only probable. (''b'') It sometimes implies that the proposition is admitted as being so reasonable that it needs no proof. (''c'') Sometimes used for religious faith.}}

{{smaller block|Knowledge and ''belief'' differ not only in degree but in kind. Knowledge is a certainty founded upon insight; ''belief'' is a certainty founded upon feeling. The one is perspicuous and objective: the other is obscure and subjective.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton'', Lectures on Logic, xxvii.}}}}

<poem>One in whom persuasion and ''belief''
Had ripened into faith, and faith become
A passionate intuition.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|They [women] persuade rather than convince, and value ''belief'' rather as a source of consolation than as a faithful expression of the reality of things.
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, II. 381.}}}}

'''4.''' That which is believed; an object of belief.

{{smaller block|Superstitious prophecies are the ''belief'' of fools.
{{right|''Bacon.''}}}}

{{smaller block|We have but to read the accounts of the early ''beliefs'' of mankind, or the present ''beliefs'' of savages and semi-cultivated nations, to see how large a field pure fiction occupies.
{{right|''G. H. Lewes'', Probs. of Life and Mind, II. iii. § 7.}}}}

33

{{smaller block|In the cathedrals, the popular ''beliefs'', hopes, fears, fancies, and aspirations found expression and were perpetuated in a language intelligible to all.
{{right|''C. E. Norton'', Travel and Study in Italy, p. 105.}}}}

'''5.''' The whole body of tenets held by the professors of any faith.

{{smaller block|In the heat of persecution, to which the Christian ''belief'' was subject, upon its first promulgation.
{{right|''Hooker.''}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''belief'' of Christianity is a ''belief'' in the beauty of holiness; the creed of Hellas was a ''belief'' in the beauty of the world and of mankind.
{{right|''Keary'', Prim. Belief, iv.}}}}

'''6.''' A creed; a formula embodying the essential doctrines of a religion or a church.

{{smaller block|Ye ought to see them have their ''belief'', to know the commandments of God, to keep their holy-days, and not to lose their time in idleness.
{{right|''Latimer'', Sermons, p. 14.}}}}

{{smaller|='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' ''Opinion'', ''Conviction'', etc. (see ''persuasion''); credence, trust, credit, confidence.—'''4.''' Doctrine.}}

'''beliefful''' (bē-lēf′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''bilefful'', < ''bilef'', ''beleve'', belief, + ''-ful''. Cf. AS. ''geleáfful''.]   Having belief or faith.   ''Udall.'' [Rare.]

'''belieffulness''' (bē-lēf′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ''beliefful'' + ''-ness''.]   The state of being beliefful. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The godly ''belieffulness'' of the heathen.
{{right|''Udall'', On Luke iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|There is a hopefulness and a ''belieffulness'', so to say, on your side, which is a great compensation.
{{right|''Clough.''}}}}

'''belier''' (bē-lī′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''belie''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who belies.

{{smaller block|Foul-mouthed ''beliers'' of the Christian faith.
{{right|''Coleridge'', Aids to Reflection, i. 89.}}}}

'''believability''' (bē-lē-va-bil′i-ti), ''n.''   [< ''believable'': see ''-bility''.]   Credibility; capability of being believed.   ''J. S. Mill.''

'''believable''' (bē-lē′va-bl), ''a.''   [< ''believe'' + ''-able.'']   Capable of being believed; credible.
{{smaller block|That he sinn’d, is not ''believable.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}

'''believableness''' (bē-lē′va̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' Credibility.

'''believe''' (bē-lēv′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''believed'', ppr. ''believing.''   [Early mod. E. ''beleeve'', < ME. ''beleven'', ''bileven'', ''bilefen'', with prefix ''be-'' (as in ''belief'', q. v.), parallel with the earlier ''leven'', by apheresis for ''ileven'', < AS. ''geliéfan'', ''gelýfan'', ''gelēfan'' = OS. ''gilōbhian'' = D. ''gelooven'' = MLG. ''gelöven'' = OHG. ''gilouben'', MHG. ''gelouben'', ''glöuben'', G. ''gleuben'', now ''glauben'', = Goth. ''galaubjan'', believe, lit. hold dear or valuable or satisfactory, be pleased with, < Goth. ''galaubs'', dear, valuable (found only in the special sense of ‘costly’), < ''ga-'' (AS., etc., ''ge-''), a generalizing prefix, + *''laub'', a form (pret.) of the common Teut. root *''lub'', whence also Goth. ''liubs'' = AS. ''leóf'', E. ''lief'', dear, AS. ''lufu'', E. ''love'', etc.: see ''lief'', ''leave''<sup>2</sup>, ''love'', ''liberal'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To have faith or confidence. {{smaller|(''a'') As to a person, to have confidence in his honesty, integrity, virtue, powers, ability, etc.; trust. (''b'') As to a thing, to have faith in its existence, or in its genuineness, efficacy, virtue, usefulness, soundness, and the like; credit its reality: as, to ''believe'' in ghosts; to ''believe'' in the Bible, in manhood suffrage, in the ballot, in republicanism, in education, etc.: usually with ''in'' or ''on'' (formerly also with ''to''), rarely absolutely.}}
{{smaller block|He saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only ''believe.''
{{right|Mark v. 36.}}}}
'''2.''' To exercise trust or confidence; rely through faith: generally with ''on.''

{{smaller block|And they said, ''Believe on'' the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house. {{right|Acts xvi. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|And many ''believed on'' him there. {{right|John x. 42.}}}}
{{smaller block|To them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that ''believe on'' his name. {{right|John i. 12.}}}}
'''3.''' To be persuaded of the truth of anything; accept a doctrine, principle, system, etc., as true, or as an object of faith: with ''in:'' as, “I ''believe in'' the Holy Ghost, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints,” etc., ''Apostles’ Creed;'' to ''believe in'' Buddhism. See ''belief.''
{{smaller block|If you will consider the nature of man, you will find that with him it always has been and still is true, that that thing in all his inward or outward world which he sees worthy of worship is essentially the thing ''in'' which he ''believes.'' {{right|''Keary'', Prim. Belief, i.}}}}

'''To make believe.''' {{smaller|See ''make''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To credit upon the ground of authority, testimony, argument, or any other ground than complete demonstration; accept as true; give credence to. See ''belief.''
{{smaller block|We know what rests upon reason; we ''believe'' what rests upon authority. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Our senses are sceptics, and ''believe'' only the impression of the moment. {{right|''Emerson'', Farming.}}}}
{{smaller block|We may ''believe'' what goes beyond our experience, only when it is inferred from that experience by the assumption that what we do not know is like what we know. {{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, II. 210.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who knows not what to ''believe''
Since he sees nothing clear.</poem>
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Empedocles.}}}}

'''2.''' To give credence to (a person making a statement, anything said, etc.).
{{smaller block|Lo, I come unto thee in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with thee, and ''believe'' thee for ever.
{{right|Ex. xix. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|You are now bound to ''believe'' him.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., v. 1.}}}}

'''3.''' To expect or hope with confidence; trust. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|I had fainted unless I had ''believed'' to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.
{{right|Ps. xxvii. 13.}}}}

'''4.''' To be of opinion; think; understand: as, I ''believe'' he has left the city.
{{smaller block|They are, I ''believe'', as high as most steeples in England.
{{right|''Addison'', Travels in Italy.}}}}

'''believer''' (bẹ̄-lē′vėr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''beleever'', ''belever'' (not in ME. or AS.); < ''believe'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who believes; one who gives credit to other evidence than that of personal knowledge; one who is firmly persuaded in his own mind of the truth or existence of something: as, a ''believer'' in ghosts.
{{smaller block|Johnson, incredulous on all other points, was a ready ''believer'' in miracles and apparitions.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Von Ranke.}}}}

'''2.''' An adherent of a religious faith; in a more restricted sense, a Christian; one who exercises faith in Christ.
{{smaller block|And ''believers'' were the more added to the Lord.
{{right|Acts v. 14.}}}}

'''3.''' In the early church, a baptized layman, in contradistinction to the clergy on the one hand, and to the catechumens, who were preparing for baptism, on the other.

{{smaller block|The name ''believer'' is here taken in a more strict sense only for one order of Christians, the believing or baptized laity. {{right|''Bingham'', Antiquities, I. iii. 1.}}}}

'''believing''' (bē-lē′ving), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Having faith; ready or disposed to believe or to exercise faith.

{{smaller block|Be not faithless, but ''believing''. {{right|John xx. 27.}}}}

<poem>Now, God be prais’d! that to ''believing'' souls
Gives light in darkness, comfort in despair.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 1.}}

'''2.''' Of the number of those who are disciples.

{{smaller block|And they that have ''believing'' masters, let them not despise them, because they are brethren. {{right|1 Tim. vi. 2.}}}}

'''believingly''' (bē-lē′ving-li), ''adv.'' In a believing manner; with belief: as, to receive a doctrine ''believingly''.

'''belight''' (bē-līt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''light''<sup>1</sup>.]   To light up; illuminate.   ''Cowley.'' [Rare.]

'''belike''' (bē-līk′), ''adv.''   [First in early mod. E., also written ''belyke'', ''bylyke''; also ''belikely'', q. v.; appar. of dial. origin, < ''be'', ''by'', prep., + ''like'', ''likely'', i. e., by what is likely; but perhaps a reduction of an introductory phrase ''it may be'' (or ''will be'') ''like'' or ''likely''. Cf. ''maybe'' and ''likely'', as similarly used.]   Perhaps; probably. [Now chiefly poetical.]

<poem>Then you, ''belike'', suspect these noblemen
As guilty of Duke Humphrey’s timeless death.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}

{{smaller block|''Belike'' this is some new kind of subscription the gallants use. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, iii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|If he came in for a reckoning, ''belike'' it was for better treat than mine. {{right|''Scott.''}}}}

'''belikely†''' (bẹ̄-līk′li), ''adv.''   [See ''belike.'']   Probably.

{{smaller block|Having ''belikely'' heard some better words of me than I could deserve. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Account of Himself.}}}}

'''belime''' (bẹ̄-līm′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''lime''<sup>1</sup>.]   To besmear or entangle with or as with bird-lime.   ''Bp. Hall.''

'''belinkedness''' (bẹ̄-lingkt′nes), ''n.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''link''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ness.'']   In ''math.'', the number of times one branch of a link must be passed through the other in order to undo it.

'''belittle''' (bẹ̄-lit′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''belittled'', ppr. ''belittling.''   [First in U. S.; < ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''little.'']   '''1.''' To make small or smaller; reduce in proportion or extent. [Rare.]—'''2.''' To cause to appear small; depreciate; lower in character or importance; speak lightly or disparagingly of.

'''belittlement''' (bẹ̄-lit′l-ment), ''n.''   [< ''belittle'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of belittling, or detracting from the character or importance of a person or thing.

{{smaller block|A systematic ''belittlement'' of the essential, and exaggeration of the non-essential, in the story. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XX. 370.}}}}

'''belive<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v. i.''   [ME. (rare), < AS. ''belīfan'' (pret. ''belāf'', pl. ''belifon'', pp. ''belifen'') (= OS. ''bilībhan'' = OFries. ''bilīva'', ''blīva'' = D. ''blijven'' = OHG. ''bilīban'', MHG. ''belīben'', ''blīben'', G. ''bleiben'' = Goth. ''bileiban''), remain, < ''be-'' + *''līfan'' (pret. ''lāf''), remain. Hence the causal ''beleave'', q. v., now also obsolete: see ''leave''<sup>1</sup>.]   To remain.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
